guided.title: Modes to octal
guided.prompt: The functions `mode_to_octal`, `octal_to_mode` and `apply_chmod` are given. Print `mode_to_octal` of `rwxr-xr-x`, `rw-r-----` and `r--------`, one result per line.
hints: Each call returns an integer such as 754.

guided.title: Octal to modes
guided.prompt: Print `octal_to_mode` of 600, 644 and 750 on one line each, in that order.
hints: octal_to_mode takes an integer such as 644.
Use a list and a for loop.

guided.title: Symbolic chmod
guided.prompt: Using `apply_chmod`, print the octal mode that results from applying `u+x` to 644, `go-r` to 755 and `a=rx` to 600, one per line.
hints: Each call needs an octal number and a clause string.
The result is an integer, for example 744.
Three print calls with the three pairs.

independent.title: Audit world-writable files
independent.prompt: `listing` holds mode and name per line. Print, in the order given, each file whose mode gives *others* the write permission, as `name: <octal now> -> <octal after chmod o-w>`. Skip files that others cannot write. Use the given functions. Print nothing for files that are fine.

independent.title: Default modes from a umask
independent.prompt: Write `default_modes(umask)` that returns the tuple `(file_mode, dir_mode)` as three-digit integers, where the file mode is 666 and the directory mode is 777 with the umask bits removed digit by digit (a digit of the umask clears those bits in the same digit). Print `umask file dir` for umasks 22, 77 and 2 formatted as three-digit strings, for example `022 644 755`, one per line.

independent.title: Parallel loads with wait
independent.prompt: Write a Bash script outline that starts three loads (`load_a.sh`, `load_b.sh`, `load_c.sh`) in the background, waits for each by PID, prints which ones failed and exits 1 if any failed, otherwise exits 0. Explain why plain `wait` is not enough.
independent.solution:
```text
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -uo pipefail
failed=0
pids=()
for job in load_a.sh load_b.sh load_c.sh; do
  ./"$job" &
  pids+=($!)
done
i=0
for job in load_a.sh load_b.sh load_c.sh; do
  if ! wait "${pids[$i]}"; then
    echo "failed: $job"
    failed=1
  fi
  i=$((i + 1))
done
exit $failed
```

Plain `wait` with no argument returns 0 once all jobs have ended, whatever their statuses, so a failed load would be missed. `wait $pid` returns the status of that one job. `set -e` is left off so that the script can collect all failures and report them before it exits.
rubric: Starts each job with & and records its PID from $!.
Waits for each PID separately and tests its status.
Exits non-zero when any job failed.
Explains that plain wait hides failures.

environment.note: The bash examples need a Unix shell with Bash, find, du and coreutils (macOS, Linux or WSL) and run in a throwaway folder; they are shown read-only in the browser with the output produced when the lesson was tested. Signals, background jobs and umask behave the same way on your own machine; PIDs and owners differ, which is why no example prints them. The mode arithmetic is modelled by Python functions that are graded in the browser.

checks.question: A background job is stopped with kill (default signal). What does `wait $pid` report?
checks.explanation: A process ended by a signal reports 128 plus the signal number; the default signal is SIGTERM (15), so 143. 9 would be the signal number of SIGKILL, not an exit status.

checks.question: What is the octal form of rwxr-x---?
checks.explanation: rwx is 7, r-x is 5, --- is 0. 755 would give others read and execute; 640 is rw-r-----.

checks.question: With umask 077, a new file is created. Which mode does it get?
checks.explanation: New files start from 666 and the umask removes bits: 666 minus 077 is 600. rwx------ would need the execute bit, which files never receive by default.

checks.question: A script starts three jobs with & and immediately runs `cat out*.txt`. What is the likely symptom?
options: Some files are missing or empty because the jobs have not finished
checks.explanation: Background jobs run concurrently with the script. Without wait the cat can run first. cat has no idea about other processes.

checks.question: Why is `kill -9` a last resort?
options: The process cannot catch it, so its trap or cleanup never runs
checks.explanation: SIGKILL cannot be caught, so temporary files and locks may be left behind. SIGTERM lets the program clean up first.
